title: A Doll Like Me
sub: PreK–Kindergarten · The Importance of Black Barbie
objective: Children will notice that people, and dolls, look different in many ways, and that every child should be able to find a doll that looks like them. They will hear that the first Black Barbie, made in 1980, was designed by Kitty Black Perkins, a Black fashion designer, with natural hairstyles, Afrocentric facial features and a glamorous design that celebrated Black beauty. Then they will design a doll of their own.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: A doll that looks like you says: you are beautiful just as you are. In 1980 the first Black Barbie said that to many Black children.

items.text: name ways that people, and dolls, can look different: skin, hair, clothes, glasses

materials: Three or four dolls or toy figures from your classroom, as different from one another as you have
The *Who Do You See?* room on a screen, open at **Design a doll**
The *Show your class* page (page 3), projected or printed
Crayons in many skin and hair colors, and the differentiated handouts
questions: How many dolls can you see? Let’s count them together.
How are these dolls different from each other? How are they the same?
Who designed the first Black Barbie?
If you designed a doll, what would it look like?
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** look at poster 2, *The Importance of Black Barbie*, together. Count the circles. What colors can you find?
**Virtual visit:** in *Who Do You See?*, the **Design a doll** tab lets children choose skin, hair, clothes, glasses, a hearing aid or a wheelchair.

steps.title: Who do our dolls look like?
script: Sit in a circle and set the classroom dolls in the middle. Let the children look, then ask: *“How are these dolls the same? How are they different?”* Collect their words: hair, skin, eyes, clothes, size. Then wonder aloud: *“What if every doll in the toy shop looked exactly the same? Who would be left out?”*

screen.question: Who do our dolls look like?

steps.purpose: Look at real dolls before any story, and notice how they are alike and different.
students: How are they the same? How are they different?

steps.title: The first Black Barbie
script: Tell the story simply. *“A long time ago, in 1980, a toy company called Mattel made a new doll: the very first Black Barbie. A woman named Kitty Black Perkins designed her. A designer is the person who decides how something will look. Kitty Black Perkins was a Black fashion designer. She gave the doll natural hairstyles, and a glamorous design that celebrated Black beauty.”*

screen.text:
The first Black Barbie
1980
Designed by Kitty Black Perkins

steps.purpose: Hear the true story: a designer made a doll so Black children could see themselves.

steps.title: A doll like me
script: Then ask the poster’s own question: *“Why do you think it matters for children to see toys that look like them?”* Let children answer with a partner, then share. Help them to the idea: *every child should be able to find a doll that looks like them, and dolls that look like everyone help us all feel we belong.*

screen.question: Why do you think it matters for children to see toys that look like them?

steps.purpose: Turn the story into the big idea: every child deserves a doll that looks like them.

steps.title: So many kinds of hair
script: Show the hairstyles from the *Design a doll* tab: an Afro, Afro puffs, Bantu knots, box braids, cornrows, locs and twists. *“The first Black Barbie had natural hair. Which of these have you seen? Which would you choose for a doll?”* If you have time, choose one or two things together in **Design a doll** (skin, hair, glasses, clothes) and watch the doll change.

steps.title: Your handout
script: Each child works on a handout. All three show the same dolls, and all three end with a doll the child designs.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Picture-led. Count the dolls and circle the number, circle the doll who wears glasses, color a doll to look like you or someone you love, and trace *ME*.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: A little more. Count the dolls, draw a different hairstyle on each of three dolls, color a doll of their own, and copy *ME* under a model.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Draw and tell. Tell a grown-up how the dolls are different, design a doll of their own from head to toe, and finish *My doll has…* aloud or in writing.

steps.purpose: Notice differences and design a doll on paper, at the right level for each child.
students: Find the dolls on your page. Then make a doll of your own.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the questions on the screen. For each one, the children show a thumb up, sideways or down: *“Can you now name ways that people and dolls can look different? Can you say why every child needs a doll like them? Can you design a doll and tell us about it?”*

steps.title: Share your doll
script: Then say: *“Hold up your doll. Tell a partner one thing about it: its hair, its clothes, or something special.”* Finish with a celebration: *every doll here looks like someone, and every one of you belongs.*
